Ankles
ăng´klz
n. pl. (the joints between leg and foot)
From the Saxon ancleow. The word stands once in the KJV text proper, and it marks the first of four measurements in Ezekiel's vision of the river that runs from the temple.

Biblical Definition

A man with a measuring line leads the prophet into a river, and the depth is recorded at each thousand cubits: “And when the man that had the line in his hand went forth eastward, he measured a thousand cubits, and he brought me through the waters; the waters were to the ankles” (Ezekiel 47:3). The ankles are the shallow end, and they are the point. The river does not begin as a torrent; it begins as water a man can wade without effort, and it grows by measured stages: “Again he measured a thousand, and brought me through the waters; the waters were to the knees. Again he measured a thousand, and brought me through; the waters were to the loins” (Ezekiel 47:4). At the fourth thousand the wading stops: “Afterward he measured a thousand; and it was a river that I could not pass over: for the waters were risen, waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over” (Ezekiel 47:5). The river is not fed by tributaries; it issues from the sanctuary and deepens on its own, and what it touches lives: “And it shall come to pass, that every thing that liveth, which moveth, whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live: and there shall be a very great multitude of fish, because these waters shall come thither: for they shall be healed; and every thing shall live whither the river cometh” (Ezekiel 47:9). The measurement at the ankles is where a reader stands at the beginning.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines ankle as the joint which connects the foot with the leg.

expand to see more

ANKLE, n. [Sax. ancleow.] The joint which connects the foot with the leg.

FORD, v.t. To pass a river or other water by treading or walking on the bottom.

RIVER, n. A large stream of water flowing in a channel on land toward the ocean, a lake or another river.

SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; the most retired part of the temple, where the ark was kept.

HEAL, v.t. To cure of a disease or wound and restore to soundness; to reconcile, as a breach.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 47:3 — "And when the man that had the line in his hand went forth eastward, he measured a thousand cubits, and he brought me through the waters; the waters were to the ankles."

Ezekiel 47:4 — "Again he measured a thousand, and brought me through the waters; the waters were to the knees. Again he measured a thousand, and brought me through; the waters were to the loins."

Ezekiel 47:5 — "Afterward he measured a thousand; and it was a river that I could not pass over: for the waters were risen, waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over."

Ezekiel 47:9 — "And it shall come to pass, that every thing that liveth, which moveth, whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live: and there shall be a very great multitude of fish, because these waters shall come thither: for they shall be healed; and every thing shall live whither the river cometh."

Modern Corruption

The rising river is turned into a metaphor for the believer's deepening spiritual experience, which relocates the source of the water from the sanctuary to the self.

expand to see more

The most common devotional use of Ezekiel 47 makes the four depths four stages of Christian maturity: ankle-deep believers who want more, and the challenge to go out further until one is swimming. The exhortation may be well meant, but it inverts the vision. Ezekiel is not choosing his depth; a man with a line is measuring and leading him, and the water is rising because of what it flows from, not because of the prophet's appetite. The river issues from under the threshold of the house. Its increase is a property of its source. Reading it as a chart of personal zeal quietly moves the miracle from the sanctuary into the worshipper.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the direction of the flow. Everything in the chapter moves outward and downward from the temple to the desert and to the Dead Sea, and what is healed is healed because the water arrived, not because it deserved water. The waters go into the sea and the sea is healed. That is the gospel's own shape, and it is why the New Testament closes with a river proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb. The believer's part in Ezekiel 47 is to be led in and to be one of the living things the river reached.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ophes (H657), the ankles; berek (H1290), the knees; nachal (H5158), a stream or river; raphah (H7495), to heal.

expand to see more

Hebrew ophes (H657) — the ankles; the first measured depth, Ezekiel 47:3.

Hebrew berek (H1290) — the knees; the second thousand cubits.

Hebrew mothen (H4975) — the loins; the third measure before the water becomes impassable.

Hebrew nachal (H5158) — a torrent, stream; the river issuing from the sanctuary.

Hebrew raphah (H7495) — to heal, mend; the waters shall be healed.

Usage

"“The waters were to the ankles” — the first of four measurements."

"“A river that I could not pass over” — the fourth thousand cubits."

"“Every thing shall live whither the river cometh” — the effect of the water."
